paper.title: SPARD: Defending Harmful Fine-Tuning Attack via Safety Projection with Relevance-Diversity Data Selection

read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1-5; appendices (derivation, DPP complexity, transformation prompts, comparison with prior selection work) skimmed

claims.claim: An aligned language model can be fine-tuned on a downstream task contaminated with harmful examples while keeping its safety, by alternating ordinary task updates with explicit corrective steps that push the parameters back whenever the loss on a small set of safe refusal examples rises above a threshold, where that safe set is chosen to be both relevant to the task data and diverse. Supported only if, with 10% harmful examples injected from each of four harmful datasets, it gives the lowest average attack success rate of all compared defences (plain fine-tuning, re-adding safety prompts at inference, mixing in random safe data, proximal bi-state training, gradient-conflict projection) for two model families on a math task and for a second task (science QA), while keeping task accuracy within about 2 points of plain fine-tuning; and if it also works with full-parameter fine-tuning, not just adapters, at small extra training cost.
claims.decision_rule: Lowest avg ASR vs SFT, PTST, SafeInstr, Lisa, SafeGrad on GSM8K (Qwen-7B, Llama-3B) and OpenBookQA (Qwen-7B); accuracy within ~2 pts of SFT; lowest ASR under full FT; modest overhead.

claims.claim: In defences that use a small set of safe examples against harmful fine-tuning, which safe examples are used matters a great deal: examples similar to the fine-tuning data protect far better than random ones, but choosing only the most similar ones loses coverage of other harmful behaviours, so selection should balance relevance and diversity. Supported only if attack success falls steeply as the average similarity of the safe set to the fine-tuning data rises and then rises again at the highest similarity; and if, with the same training procedure, a relevance-and-diversity selection gives at least 5 points lower average attack success than both random selection and taking the most similar examples, without lower task accuracy.
claims.decision_rule: U-shaped ASR vs similarity (68.8% -> 11.4% -> 16.6%); R-D DPP avg ASR >= 5 pts below random and max-quality selection with equal or higher accuracy.

experiments.text: Set up the attack and evaluation. Setup: four harmful corpora, each split 90/10: BeaverTails QA, BeaverTails rewritten as instructions, LatHarmful instructions, and LatHarmful rewritten as QA (rewrites by GPT-4o-mini). Harmful queries with harmful answers from the training splits are injected into the downstream data at 10% of its size; harmful queries with safe answers form the pool of candidate safe examples. Downstream tasks GSM8K (augmented with MetaMath) and OpenBookQA; models Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct with LoRA (rank 32), AdamW, learning rate 5e-5. Safety is judged by GPT-4o-mini on the test splits' harmful queries with a 1-5 harmfulness score; attack success is the share scoring above 2.

Define the defence. Setup: after each task gradient step, compute the loss on a mini-batch of selected safe examples; if it exceeds a threshold (0.2, set from the aligned model's own safety loss), project the parameters onto the linearised half-space where the safety loss meets the threshold, capping the step at a trust-region radius equal to the learning rate. Select safe examples equal to 3% of the fine-tuning data by greedy determinantal-point-process selection with a kernel combining similarity between candidates (for diversity) and each candidate's maximum cosine similarity to the fine-tuning data raised to power 4 (for relevance), using mean final-layer embeddings of the pretrained model.

Compare defences on GSM8K for two model families. Result (average attack success over the four attacks / accuracy): Qwen-7B: plain fine-tuning 87.93% / 86.77%, inference-time safety prompt 74.64% / 85.06%, random safe mixing 73.59% / 86.28%, proximal bi-state training 19.12% / 78.45%, gradient-conflict projection 30.18% / 85.71%, the projection defence 9.45% / 85.77%, below even the un-fine-tuned model's 19.02%. LLaMA-3B: 91.36% / 72.27%, 79.48%, 82.01%, 24.19% / 65.03%, 71.77% / 64.29%, and 12.09% / 71.23%. It is not lowest on every single attack: the bi-state method is lower on LLaMA LatHarmful (9.90% vs 11.31%).

Repeat on a science QA task and with full fine-tuning. Setup: OpenBookQA with Qwen-7B under the same four attacks; and full-parameter fine-tuning of SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct on GSM8K under the BeaverTails attack. Result: OpenBookQA average attack success 14.54% against 40.29% (plain), 30.30%, 41.69%, 18.80% (bi-state) and 20.63%, with accuracy 83.25% against 83.70% for plain fine-tuning; full fine-tuning 17.4% against 74.0% plain, 69.0% bi-state and 23.2% gradient-conflict projection, at 50.6% vs 51.5% accuracy.

Check the role of the step cap and the cost. Setup: remove the trust-region cap on the projection step; measure end-to-end wall-clock time on one A800 for Qwen-7B on GSM8K; sweep the safe-set ratio, the threshold and the relevance exponent under the BeaverTails attack. Result: without the cap, average attack success falls further to 5.03% but accuracy drops to 81.92%; total time is 273.5 minutes against 253.0 for plain fine-tuning (+8.1%), versus +9.8% for the bi-state method and +54.2% for gradient-conflict projection, with embedding extraction 3.42 minutes and selection 0.12 seconds; attack success is above 80% with no safe data and lowest at 3-5%, and thresholds above 0.5 let it rise again.

Vary how similar the safe examples are to the fine-tuning data. Setup: GSM8K merged with 10% BeaverTails attack data; safe sets drawn from the BeaverTails and LatHarmful pools at controlled average cosine similarity to the fine-tuning data. Result: attack success falls from 68.8% at low similarity to 11.4% at moderate-to-high similarity, then rises to 16.6% at about 0.94 average similarity, where the selected examples cover only a narrow region of harmful behaviour.

Hold the training procedure fixed and change only the selection. Setup: Qwen-7B on GSM8K under the four attacks with the projection defence using random safe examples, the highest-similarity examples, or relevance-and-diversity selection. Result: average attack success 15.85% (random), 16.51% (most similar) and 9.45%, with accuracy 85.06%, 85.69% and 85.77%; even random selection beats the bi-state method (19.12%). A t-SNE view shows random sets spread away from the attack distribution and most-similar sets clustered tightly on it, while the balanced set lies near it but spread out; 69% of candidates already have similarity above 0.9, which is why relevance is raised to a power.

dropped: Derivation of the projection step and DPP complexity (theory).
notes: Effects of p, tau and beta are shown only as figures; experiment text gives the qualitative pattern stated in the paper.
